title: Oracle SQL Reviewer Question Bank 51-100 (Corrected v2)
description: Corrected question bank with restored tables, queries, outputs, source-highlighted scoring, understandable per-choice explanations, and explicit technical notes for disputed items.

questions.stem: Which three queries execute successfully?

options.text: SELECT 1 - SYSDATE - DATE '2019-01-01' FROM dual;
options.explanation: Oracle cannot subtract a DATE value from the number 1.

options.text: SELECT SYSDATE - DATE '2019-01-01' - 1 FROM dual;
options.explanation: Subtracting two dates returns the number of days between them. Oracle can then subtract 1 from that numeric result.

options.text: SELECT SYSDATE / DATE '2019-01-01' - 1 FROM dual;
options.explanation: Oracle does not support division between two DATE values.

options.text: SELECT SYSDATE - 1 - DATE '2019-01-01' FROM dual;
options.explanation: SYSDATE - 1 produces the date one day earlier. Subtracting another date then returns the difference in days.

options.text: SELECT (SYSDATE - DATE '2019-01-01') / 7 FROM dual;
options.explanation: Subtracting the dates returns a numeric day difference, which can then be divided by 7.

options.text: SELECT 1 / SYSDATE - DATE '2019-01-01' FROM dual;
options.explanation: A number cannot be divided by a DATE value.

questions.answerExplanation: Subtracting two dates returns the number of days between them. Oracle can then subtract 1 from that numeric result. SYSDATE - 1 produces the date one day earlier. Subtracting another date then returns the difference in days. Subtracting the dates returns a numeric day difference, which can then be divided by 7.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about scalar subquery expressions?

options.text: They can be nested.
options.explanation: A scalar subquery can contain another subquery when the syntax and nesting context permit it.

options.text: They cannot be used in the VALUES clause of an INSERT statement.
options.explanation: A scalar subquery can be used as a value in an INSERT statement when it returns no more than one row and one column.

options.text: A scalar subquery expression that returns zero rows evaluates to zero.
options.explanation: A scalar subquery that returns no rows evaluates to NULL, not zero.

options.text: They can be used as default values for columns in a CREATE TABLE statement.
options.explanation: Scalar subqueries cannot be used as column default expressions in a CREATE TABLE statement.

options.text: A scalar subquery expression that returns zero rows evaluates to NULL.
options.explanation: When the scalar subquery returns no row, Oracle represents its result as NULL.

options.text: They cannot be used in GROUP BY clauses.
options.explanation: Oracle does not permit scalar subquery expressions as expressions in a GROUP BY clause.

questions.answerExplanation: A scalar subquery can contain another subquery when the syntax and nesting context permit it. When the scalar subquery returns no row, Oracle represents its result as NULL. Oracle does not permit scalar subquery expressions as expressions in a GROUP BY clause.

SELECT deptno AS "Department",
       AVG(sal) AS AverageSalary,
       MAX(sal) AS "Max Salary"
FROM emp
WHERE sal >= 12000
GROUP BY "Department"
ORDER BY AverageSalary;

options.text: An alias name must not contain space characters.
options.explanation: An alias may contain spaces when the alias is enclosed in double quotation marks, such as "Max Salary".

options.text: An alias name must always be specified in quotes.
options.explanation: Quotation marks are optional for ordinary aliases such as AverageSalary. They are required when preserving case or including spaces and special characters.

options.text: An alias name must not be used in an ORDER BY clause.
options.explanation: A select-list alias may be used in the ORDER BY clause. Therefore, ORDER BY AverageSalary is valid.

options.text: An alias name must not be used in a GROUP BY clause.
options.explanation: In this Oracle SQL context, the GROUP BY clause must use the underlying expression or column name, such as GROUP BY deptno, instead of the select-list alias "Department".

questions.answerExplanation: In this Oracle SQL context, the GROUP BY clause must use the underlying expression or column name, such as GROUP BY deptno, instead of the select-list alias "Department".

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about Oracle synonyms?

options.text: A synonym cannot be created for a PL/SQL package.
options.explanation: A synonym can be created for a stored PL/SQL package.

options.text: A synonym can be available to all users.
options.explanation: A public synonym can be referenced by database users, subject to the required privileges on the underlying object.

options.text: A sequence can have a synonym.
options.explanation: Oracle permits a private or public synonym to reference a sequence.

options.text: A synonym created by one user can refer to an object belonging to another user.
options.explanation: A synonym can reference an object in another schema by using the schema-qualified object name.

questions.answerExplanation: A public synonym can be referenced by database users, subject to the required privileges on the underlying object. Oracle permits a private or public synonym to reference a sequence. A synonym can reference an object in another schema by using the schema-qualified object name.

questions.stem: You create a table named 123. Which statement runs successfully?

options.text: SELECT * FROM TABLE(123);
options.explanation: The TABLE operator is used with collection expressions or table functions, not as a way to reference a table with a numeric name.

options.text: SELECT * FROM "123";
options.explanation: An object name beginning with a number must be created and referenced as a quoted identifier using double quotation marks.

options.text: SELECT * FROM \123\;
options.explanation: Backslashes are not valid delimiters for Oracle object identifiers.

options.text: SELECT * FROM '123';
options.explanation: Single quotation marks identify a character literal, not a table or other database object.

questions.answerExplanation: An object name beginning with a number must be created and referenced as a quoted identifier using double quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about queries using set operators (UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and MINUS)?

options.text: The name of each column in the first SELECT list must match the name of the corresponding column in each subsequent SELECT list.
options.explanation: Corresponding columns do not need identical names. The final result uses the column names from the first SELECT.

options.text: None of the set operators can be used when selecting CLOB columns.
options.explanation: This statement is too broad. Restrictions depend on the specific set operator and data type involved.

options.text: There must be an equal number of columns in each SELECT list.
options.explanation: Every query combined by a set operator must return the same number of columns.

options.text: Each SELECT statement in the query can have an ORDER BY clause.
options.explanation: Individual component queries cannot each have an ORDER BY. A single ORDER BY may be placed at the end of the complete compound query.

options.text: The FOR UPDATE clause cannot be specified.
options.explanation: The FOR UPDATE clause is not permitted in a query that uses set operators.

questions.answerExplanation: Every query combined by a set operator must return the same number of columns. The FOR UPDATE clause is not permitted in a query that uses set operators.

questions.stem: The INVOICE table has a QTY_SOLD column of data type NUMBER and an INVOICE_DATE column of data type DATE. NLS_DATE_FORMAT is set to DD-MON-RR. Which two statements are true about data type conversions involving these columns in query expressions?

options.text: invoice_date = '15-MARCH-2019' uses implicit conversion.
options.explanation: Oracle must implicitly convert the character string into a DATE value before comparing it with INVOICE_DATE.

options.text: qty_sold BETWEEN '101' AND '110' uses implicit conversion.
options.explanation: Oracle implicitly converts the character values '101' and '110' to numbers before comparing them with the numeric column.

options.text: invoice_date > '01-02-2019' uses implicit conversion.
options.explanation: Although implicit conversion would be attempted, the character value does not match the specified DD-MON-RR date format because the month is numeric rather than an abbreviated month name.

options.text: qty_sold = '0554982' requires explicit conversion.
options.explanation: Oracle can implicitly convert a valid numeric character string to NUMBER for comparison with QTY_SOLD.

options.text: CONCAT(qty_sold, invoice_date) requires explicit conversion.
options.explanation: Oracle can implicitly convert the numeric and date values to character values for CONCAT.

questions.answerExplanation: Oracle must implicitly convert the character string into a DATE value before comparing it with INVOICE_DATE. Oracle implicitly converts the character values '101' and '110' to numbers before comparing them with the numeric column.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about the Oracle join syntax and ANSI join syntax?

options.text: The Oracle join syntax supports creation of a Cartesian product of two tables.
options.explanation: Listing two tables without a join condition produces every possible combination of rows from the two tables.

options.text: The Oracle join syntax only supports right outer joins.
options.explanation: Oracle’s traditional join syntax can represent left and right outer joins using the (+) operator.

options.text: The SQL:1999-compliant ANSI join syntax supports creation of a Cartesian product of two tables.
options.explanation: ANSI syntax supports Cartesian products through CROSS JOIN.

options.text: The Oracle join syntax performs less well than the SQL:1999-compliant ANSI join syntax.
options.explanation: Join syntax alone does not make the query perform worse. Oracle can generate equivalent execution plans for logically equivalent joins.

options.text: The Oracle join syntax supports natural joins.
options.explanation: Oracle supports NATURAL JOIN, which joins tables automatically using identically named compatible columns.

options.text: The Oracle join syntax performs better than the SQL:1999-compliant ANSI join syntax.
options.explanation: Traditional Oracle syntax is not inherently faster than ANSI syntax. Performance depends on the execution plan and data access methods.

options.text: The SQL:1999-compliant ANSI join syntax supports natural joins.
options.explanation: This statement is also technically true because NATURAL JOIN is part of ANSI join syntax. However, the document highlights A, C, and E as its expected answers.

questions.answerExplanation: Listing two tables without a join condition produces every possible combination of rows from the two tables. ANSI syntax supports Cartesian products through CROSS JOIN. Oracle supports NATURAL JOIN, which joins tables automatically using identically named compatible columns.

questions.stem: Examine the query and its displayed output. Which GROUP BY clause must be added so the query returns the results shown?

codeBlocks.title: Incomplete query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT ch.channel_type, t.month, co.country_code,
       SUM(s.amount_sold) AS sales
FROM sales s, times t, channels ch, countries co
WHERE s.time_id = t.time_id
  AND s.country_id = co.country_id
  AND s.channel_id = ch.channel_id
  AND ch.channel_type IN ('Direct Sales', 'Internet')
  AND t.month IN ('2000-09', '2000-10')
  AND co.country_code IN ('GB', 'US')
<GROUP BY clause>
ORDER BY ch.channel_type, t.month, co.country_code;

options.text: GROUP BY ch.channel_type, ROLLUP(t.month, co.country_code)
options.explanation: The regular grouping by channel separates each channel, while ROLLUP returns month-and-country details, monthly subtotals, and a higher-level subtotal for each channel.

options.text: GROUP BY ch.channel_type, t.month, ROLLUP(co.country_code)
options.explanation: This produces country-level rows and monthly subtotals, but it does not roll up the month level within each channel.

options.text: GROUP BY CUBE(ch.channel_type, t.month, co.country_code)
options.explanation: CUBE generates every possible grouping combination, producing more subtotal combinations than those shown.

options.text: GROUP BY ch.channel_type, t.month, co.country_code
options.explanation: A standard GROUP BY returns only detailed groups and does not generate the displayed subtotal rows.

questions.answerExplanation: The regular grouping by channel separates each channel, while ROLLUP returns month-and-country details, monthly subtotals, and a higher-level subtotal for each channel.
questions.technicalNote: The incomplete query and displayed subtotal output were restored from the correction document. Blank MONTH or CO cells represent subtotal rows produced by ROLLUP.

questions.stem: Examine the descriptions of the BRICKS and BRICKS_STAGE tables. Which two queries execute successfully?

options.text: SELECT brick_id, shape FROM bricks MINUS SELECT weight, color FROM bricks_stage
options.explanation: Both queries return two columns with compatible data-type groups: a numeric first column and a character second column.

options.text: SELECT * FROM bricks MINUS SELECT * FROM bricks_stage
options.explanation: BRICKS and BRICKS_STAGE do not return the same number of columns, so the set operation fails.

options.text: SELECT shape, color FROM bricks MINUS SELECT weight, color FROM bricks_stage
options.explanation: The first corresponding columns are incompatible: SHAPE is character data, while WEIGHT is numeric.

options.text: SELECT shape, color FROM bricks MINUS SELECT color, shape FROM bricks_stage
options.explanation: Both queries return two character columns, so the corresponding data types are compatible.

options.text: SELECT shape, color, weight FROM bricks MINUS SELECT * FROM bricks_stage
options.explanation: Although the column counts match, the corresponding order causes incompatible comparisons, such as a character column being matched with the numeric WEIGHT column.

questions.answerExplanation: Both queries return two columns with compatible data-type groups: a numeric first column and a character second column. Both queries return two character columns, so the corresponding data types are compatible.
questions.technicalNote: The two table descriptions were restored as separate tables. Set-operator queries require the same column count and compatible data-type groups in corresponding positions.

questions.stem: Which three are key components of an Entity Relationship Model?

options.text: An activity
options.explanation: An activity may appear in process modeling, but it is not a core component of an Entity Relationship Model.

options.text: A table
options.explanation: A table is a relational database implementation of an entity. The conceptual ER model uses entities rather than tables.

options.text: A relationship
options.explanation: A relationship describes how two or more entities are associated with one another.

options.text: An attribute
options.explanation: An attribute represents a characteristic or property of an entity, such as a student’s name or identification number.

options.text: A unique identifier
options.explanation: A unique identifier is important for identifying entity occurrences, but the three fundamental ER model components are entities, attributes, and relationships.

options.text: An entity
options.explanation: An entity represents a distinguishable real-world object or concept about which data is stored.

questions.answerExplanation: A relationship describes how two or more entities are associated with one another. An attribute represents a characteristic or property of an entity, such as a student’s name or identification number. An entity represents a distinguishable real-world object or concept about which data is stored.

questions.stem: Examine the data in the ORDERS and INVOICES tables and the query. What rows will be returned?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM orders
INTERSECT
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM invoices;

options.text: 2, NULL
options.explanation: This row is not returned. ORDERS contains (2, NULL), but INVOICES contains (2, 01-JAN-2019), so the complete two-column rows do not match.

options.text: 1, NULL
options.explanation: This row is returned. Both query branches contain ORDER_ID 1 with a NULL ORDER_DATE. INTERSECT treats corresponding nulls as equal for duplicate comparison.

options.text: 3, NULL
options.explanation: This row is not returned. INVOICES contains (3, NULL), but ORDERS contains (3, 01-JAN-2019).
This row is not returned. INVOICES contains order 5 with 01-APR-2019 rather than 01-MAR-2019.
This row is not returned. ORDERS has (3, 01-JAN-2019), while INVOICES has (3, NULL).
This row is returned because both tables contain ORDER_ID 4 with ORDER_DATE 01-FEB-2019.

questions.answerExplanation: This row is returned. Both query branches contain ORDER_ID 1 with a NULL ORDER_DATE. INTERSECT treats corresponding nulls as equal for duplicate comparison. This row is returned because both tables contain ORDER_ID 4 with ORDER_DATE 01-FEB-2019.
questions.technicalNote: The earlier JSON incorrectly merged the INVOICES rows into the ORDERS table and used the wrong date values. The correction document shows two separate tables and highlights (1, NULL) and (4, 01-FEB-2019).

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the ORDER BY clause?

options.text: In a character sort, the values are case-sensitive.
options.explanation: Character sorting is case-sensitive, so uppercase and lowercase values may appear in different positions according to their character values.

options.text: NULLs are not included in the sort operation.
options.explanation: Rows containing null values are included. By default, nulls appear last in ascending order and first in descending order unless NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST is specified.

options.text: Numeric values are displayed in descending order if they have decimal positions.
options.explanation: Decimal positions do not determine the sorting direction. The default direction is ascending unless DESC is specified.

options.text: Column aliases can be used in the ORDER BY clause.
options.explanation: A select-list alias can be referenced by the query’s ORDER BY clause.

options.text: Only columns that are specified in the SELECT list can be used in the ORDER BY clause.
options.explanation: A query can generally sort by a column that is not displayed in the select list, subject to restrictions such as the use of DISTINCT.

questions.answerExplanation: Character sorting is case-sensitive, so uppercase and lowercase values may appear in different positions according to their character values. A select-list alias can be referenced by the query’s ORDER BY clause.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about selecting related data based on an Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)?

options.text: Rows from unrelated tables cannot be joined.
options.explanation: SQL can join tables that do not have a formally defined ERD relationship, provided a valid join condition is supplied. A Cartesian product is also possible.

options.text: Relating data from a table with data from the same table is implemented with a self-join.
options.explanation: A self-join uses separate aliases for the same table to compare or relate its rows to other rows in that table.

options.text: Implementing a relationship between two tables might require joining additional tables.
options.explanation: An intermediate or associative table may be required to relate two tables, particularly when implementing a many-to-many relationship.

options.text: Every relationship between the two tables must be implemented in a join condition.
options.explanation: A query implements only the relationships necessary to produce its required result. It does not need to include every relationship defined in the ERD.

options.text: An inner join relates rows within the same table.
options.explanation: An inner join matches rows between row sources. Relating rows from the same table specifically requires a self-join.

questions.answerExplanation: A self-join uses separate aliases for the same table to compare or relate its rows to other rows in that table. An intermediate or associative table may be required to relate two tables, particularly when implementing a many-to-many relationship.

questions.stem: Examine this query: SELECT TRUNC(ROUND(156.00, -2), -1) FROM DUAL; What is the result?

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.content:
ROUND(156.00, -2) returns 200.
ROUND first rounds 156 to the nearest hundred. TRUNC then truncates 200 to the tens position, which remains 200.

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT TRUNC(ROUND(156.00, -2), -1)
FROM dual;

options.explanation: ROUND(156, -2) does not return 150. It rounds to the nearest hundred, which is 200.
The inner ROUND returns 200, and truncating 200 to the tens position still returns 200.
This would be associated with rounding to the tens position, but the query first uses -2, which rounds to hundreds.
Since 156 is at least 150, rounding it to the nearest hundred produces 200, not 100.
The negative precision values operate on positions to the left of the decimal point. They do not divide the value by 10.

questions.answerExplanation: The inner ROUND returns 200, and truncating 200 to the tens position still returns 200.

questions.stem: Examine this SQL statement. Which two statements are true?

codeBlocks.title: SQL statement
codeBlocks.code:
DELETE FROM employees e
WHERE EXISTS
(SELECT 'dummy'
FROM emp_history
WHERE employee_id = e.employee_id);

options.text: The DELETE statement executes successfully even if the subquery selects multiple rows.
options.explanation: EXISTS checks only whether at least one matching row exists. Multiple matching rows do not cause a single-row subquery error.

options.text: The subquery is executed before the DELETE statement is executed.
options.explanation: The subquery is correlated with the current row of EMPLOYEES; it is evaluated as part of processing the DELETE.

options.text: The subquery is not a correlated subquery.
options.explanation: The reference to e.employee_id connects the subquery to the current row of the outer EMPLOYEES table.

options.text: All existing rows in the EMPLOYEES table are deleted.
options.explanation: Only employees for whom at least one matching EMP_HISTORY row exists are deleted.

options.text: The subquery is executed for every row in the EMPLOYEES table.
options.explanation: Because the subquery references e.employee_id, Oracle evaluates the correlated condition for each candidate employee row.

questions.answerExplanation: EXISTS checks only whether at least one matching row exists. Multiple matching rows do not cause a single-row subquery error. Because the subquery references e.employee_id, Oracle evaluates the correlated condition for each candidate employee row.

questions.stem: Examine the partial statement and its displayed output. Which ORDER BY clause will generate the displayed output?

codeBlocks.title: Partial statement
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT ename, sal, comm
FROM emp

options.text: ORDER BY comm DESC NULLS LAST, ename
options.explanation: Commission values are sorted from highest to lowest, followed by null commissions. Employees with null commissions are sorted alphabetically by name.

options.text: ORDER BY NVL(comm, 0) ASC NULLS FIRST, ename
options.explanation: Ascending order would place zero and null-equivalent commission values before 300 and 500.

options.text: ORDER BY NVL(comm, 0) ASC NULLS LAST, ename
options.explanation: NVL(comm, 0) converts null commissions to zero, and ascending order would place those rows first.

options.text: ORDER BY NVL(comm, 0) DESC, ename
options.explanation: This would treat TURNER’s zero commission and all null commissions as equal. Those rows would then be sorted alphabetically together, placing TURNER after the other names rather than before them.

questions.answerExplanation: Commission values are sorted from highest to lowest, followed by null commissions. Employees with null commissions are sorted alphabetically by name.
questions.technicalNote: The displayed result was converted from separate text fragments into one structured table. The output orders non-null commissions descending, then null commissions by ENAME.

questions.stem: Examine the description and contents of the CUSTOMERS table. Which two SELECT statements will return only Mandy and Mary?

options.text: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE UPPER(customer_name) LIKE '%MA%';
options.explanation: UPPER converts all names to uppercase. Every displayed name contains MA, so this returns more than Mandy and Mary.

options.text: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_name = '%Ma%';
options.explanation: The equality operator treats % as an ordinary character. It does not perform wildcard matching.

options.text: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_name LIKE 'Ma%';
options.explanation: The pattern matches case-sensitive names beginning with Ma, which returns Mandy and Mary but not the fully uppercase names.

options.text: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE UPPER(customer_name) LIKE 'MA%';
options.explanation: After conversion to uppercase, all displayed customer names begin with MA, so more than the two required rows are returned.

options.text: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_name LIKE '%Ma%';
options.explanation: This case-sensitive pattern matches names containing Ma, which returns Mandy and Mary from the displayed data.

questions.answerExplanation: The pattern matches case-sensitive names beginning with Ma, which returns Mandy and Mary but not the fully uppercase names. This case-sensitive pattern matches names containing Ma, which returns Mandy and Mary from the displayed data.

questions.stem: Examine the contents of the EMP table and the query below. What is the result?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT id, name, salary
FROM emp
ORDER BY salary
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES;

options.text: It will return the five employees earning the lowest salaries, in ascending order.
options.explanation: ORDER BY salary uses ascending order. The five lowest rows are the two salaries of 12000, followed by 17000, 18000, and 24000. Because no additional row ties with the fifth-row salary of 24000, exactly five employees are returned.

options.text: It will return the five employees earning the highest salaries, in descending order.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because DESC is not specified. Oracle sorts the salaries in ascending order, beginning with the lowest salary.

options.text: It will return the six employees earning the highest salaries, in descending order.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because the query does not sort in descending order and therefore does not return the highest salaries first.

options.text: It will return the six employees earning the lowest salaries, in ascending order.
options.explanation: This is incorrect. WITH TIES adds extra rows only when another row has the same ORDER BY value as the fifth row. No other employee has salary 24000.

questions.answerExplanation: ORDER BY salary uses ascending order. The five lowest rows are the two salaries of 12000, followed by 17000, 18000, and 24000. Because no additional row ties with the fifth-row salary of 24000, exactly five employees are returned.
questions.technicalNote: The dictated result rows and calculation were removed from the question body. The result is now derived only in the explanations after submission.

questions.stem: Examine the contents of the CUSTOMERS table. You need to display the last names and credit limits of all customers whose last name starts with A or B, in lowercase or uppercase, and whose credit limit is below 1000. Which two WHERE conditions give the required result?

codeBlocks.title: Incomplete query

options.text: WHERE (UPPER(cust_last_name) LIKE INITCAP('A') OR UPPER(cust_last_name) LIKE INITCAP('B')) AND ROUND(cust_credit_limit) < ROUND(1000);
options.explanation: INITCAP('A') and INITCAP('B') return only A and B. Without %, LIKE matches only a last name consisting of that single letter.

options.text: WHERE (UPPER(cust_last_name) LIKE 'A%' OR UPPER(cust_last_name) LIKE 'B%') AND ROUND(cust_credit_limit) < 1000;
options.explanation: UPPER makes the comparison case-insensitive, while A% and B% match names beginning with A or B. The rounded credit limit must remain below 1000.

options.text: WHERE (INITCAP(cust_last_name) LIKE 'A%' OR INITCAP(cust_last_name) LIKE 'B%') AND cust_credit_limit < 1000;
options.explanation: INITCAP makes the first character uppercase, allowing either prefix pattern to match, and the credit limit condition is applied directly.

options.text: WHERE UPPER(cust_last_name) BETWEEN UPPER('A%') AND UPPER('B%');
options.explanation: BETWEEN compares values by range. It does not interpret % as a wildcard and does not apply the credit-limit requirement.

options.text: WHERE UPPER(cust_last_name) IN ('A%', 'B%') AND cust_credit_limit < 1000;
options.explanation: IN performs equality comparisons. It does not treat % as a wildcard.

questions.answerExplanation: UPPER makes the comparison case-insensitive, while A% and B% match names beginning with A or B. The rounded credit limit must remain below 1000. INITCAP makes the first character uppercase, allowing either prefix pattern to match, and the credit limit condition is applied directly.
questions.technicalNote: The CUSTOMERS structure and incomplete query were restored from the correction document. The source image does not display a size for CUST_ID clearly enough to reproduce, so its type is retained as VARCHAR2 without an inferred length.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the MERGE statement?

options.text: The WHEN NOT MATCHED clause can be used to specify the inserts to be performed.
options.explanation: When a source row does not match a target row, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT can add the source data to the target table.

options.text: The WHEN NOT MATCHED clause can be used to specify the deletions to be performed.
options.explanation: WHEN NOT MATCHED is used for inserts, not deletes.

options.text: The WHEN MATCHED clause can be used to specify the updates to be performed.
options.explanation: When a source row matches a target row, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE can modify the target row.

options.text: The WHEN NOT MATCHED clause can be used to specify the updates to be performed.
options.explanation: An update requires a matching target row and therefore belongs in the WHEN MATCHED clause.

options.text: The WHEN MATCHED clause can be used to specify the inserts to be performed.
options.explanation: Inserts are specified under WHEN NOT MATCHED, because a matching target row already exists under WHEN MATCHED.

questions.answerExplanation: When a source row does not match a target row, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT can add the source data to the target table. When a source row matches a target row, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE can modify the target row.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about rollbacks?

options.text: If the ROLLBACK statement is used without TO SAVEPOINT, then all savepoints in the transaction are deleted.
options.explanation: A complete rollback ends the current transaction, reverses all uncommitted changes, and erases its savepoints.

options.text: Data Control Language statements, such as GRANT and REVOKE, can be rolled back.
options.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE cause implicit commits and cannot be reversed through a transaction rollback.

options.text: The ROLLBACK statement does not release locks resulting from table updates.
options.explanation: A complete rollback releases the transaction’s data locks.

options.text: A transaction interrupted by a system failure is automatically rolled back.
options.explanation: Oracle recovery automatically rolls back an uncommitted transaction interrupted by a system failure.

options.text: Data consistency is not guaranteed after a rollback.
options.explanation: Rollback restores the transaction’s changes to a consistent earlier state.

questions.answerExplanation: A complete rollback ends the current transaction, reverses all uncommitted changes, and erases its savepoints. Oracle recovery automatically rolls back an uncommitted transaction interrupted by a system failure.

options.text:
MERGE INTO new_prices n
USING products p
ON (p.prod_id = n.prod_id)
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
INSERT (n.prod_id, n.price)
VALUES (p.prod_id, p.cost * .01)
WHERE p.cost < 200;
options.explanation: Target columns in the MERGE INSERT column list must not be qualified with the target table alias.

options.text:
MERGE INTO new_prices n
USING (SELECT * FROM products WHERE cost > 150) p
ON (p.prod_id = n.prod_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
UPDATE SET n.price = p.cost * .01
DELETE WHERE p.cost < 200;
options.explanation: The statement validly updates matched rows. A matched row is deleted when the updated source row also satisfies p.cost < 200.

options.text:
MERGE INTO new_prices n
USING (SELECT * FROM products) p
ON (p.prod_id = n.prod_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
UPDATE SET n.price = p.cost * .01
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
INSERT (prod_id, price)
VALUES (p.prod_id, p.cost * .01)
WHERE p.cost < 200;
options.explanation: The statement validly updates matching products and inserts nonmatching products whose cost is below 200.

options.text:
MERGE INTO new_prices n
USING (SELECT * FROM products WHERE cost > 150) p
ON (n.prod_id = p.prod_id)
WHEN MATCHED DELETE WHERE p.cost < 200
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
INSERT (n.prod_id, n.price)
VALUES (p.prod_id, p.cost * .01);
options.explanation: A DELETE WHERE clause must follow an update inside WHEN MATCHED; it cannot appear as a standalone matched action. The insert list also improperly qualifies target columns.

questions.answerExplanation: The statement validly updates matched rows. A matched row is deleted when the updated source row also satisfies p.cost < 200. The statement validly updates matching products and inserts nonmatching products whose cost is below 200.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the EMPLOYEES table. Which two queries return all employees whose salary is greater than the average salary in their department?

options.explanation: An analytic function cannot be used directly in the WHERE clause of the same query block. It must first be calculated in a subquery or inline view.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary > ANY (
SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
);
options.explanation: This compares each salary with the averages of all departments, not specifically with the average of that employee’s department.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
);
options.explanation: The uncorrelated subquery normally returns multiple department averages, which cannot be compared using the single-row > operator.
The inline view calculates the appropriate department average for every employee. The outer query then filters employees whose salary exceeds that value.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM employees e1
WHERE salary > (
SELECT AVG(salary)
 FROM employees e2
 WHERE e1.department_id = e2.department_id
);
options.explanation: The correlated subquery calculates the average salary for the department of the current outer employee.

questions.answerExplanation: The inline view calculates the appropriate department average for every employee. The outer query then filters employees whose salary exceeds that value. The correlated subquery calculates the average salary for the department of the current outer employee.

options.text: CREATE SEQUENCE emp_seq STARTS WITH 1 CACHE;

options.text: CREATE SEQUENCE emp_seq NOCACHE;
options.explanation: This statement is correct. START WITH 1, INCREMENT BY 1, and NOCYCLE are defaults, while NOCACHE explicitly reduces gaps from lost cached values.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about TRUNCATE and DELETE?

FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
AND MIN(salary) > 6000
GROUP BY manager_id
ORDER BY MIN(salary) DESC;
options.explanation: This query is invalid because MIN(salary) is a group function and cannot be placed in WHERE. Aggregate-group filtering belongs in HAVING after GROUP BY.

options.text:
SELECT manager_id, MIN(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY manager_id
HAVING MIN(salary) > 6000
ORDER BY MIN(salary) DESC;
options.explanation: This query is technically the correctly ordered solution: WHERE removes null managers, GROUP BY forms manager groups, HAVING removes groups with minimum salary at or below 6000, and ORDER BY ... DESC sorts the highest minimum salary first. The document nevertheless highlights C.

questions.answerExplanation: This is the choice highlighted in the supplied correction document. However, it is technically invalid because HAVING appears before GROUP BY. The clauses should be GROUP BY manager_id followed by HAVING MIN(salary) > 6000.
questions.technicalNote: None of the source choices aligns cleanly with both the highlighted key and valid clause order. The document highlights C, but C places HAVING before GROUP BY and does not execute. Choice E is the technically correct Oracle SQL statement. Scoring follows the document-highlighted answer C as requested.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the BOOKS table and the requirements. Which two queries can be used?

sections.title: Requirements
items: 1. Display book titles for books purchased before January 17, 2007, costing less than 500 or more than 1000.
2. Sort the titles by purchase date, starting with the most recently purchased book.

options.text:
SELECT book_title
FROM books
WHERE (price NOT BETWEEN 500 AND 1000)
  AND (purchase_date < '17-JAN-2007')
ORDER BY purchase_date DESC;
options.explanation: This query is correct. NOT BETWEEN 500 AND 1000 selects prices below 500 or above 1000. The date condition selects purchases before January 17, 2007, and DESC sorts the newest qualifying purchase first.

options.text:
SELECT book_title
FROM books
WHERE (price < 500 OR price > 1000)
  AND (purchase_date < '17-JAN-2007')
ORDER BY purchase_date DESC;
options.explanation: This query is technically correct because the parenthesized price expressions implement the same condition as NOT BETWEEN, and the date and descending sort also match the requirements. It is not highlighted in the source document.

options.text:
SELECT book_title
FROM books
WHERE (price < 500 OR 1000)
  AND (purchase_date < '17-JAN-2007')
ORDER BY purchase_date DESC;
options.explanation: This query is highlighted in the source document, but it is technically invalid. The expression OR 1000 does not provide a Boolean condition; it should be OR price > 1000.

options.text:
SELECT book_title
FROM books
WHERE (price BETWEEN 500 AND 1000)
  AND (purchase_date < '17-JAN-2007')
ORDER BY purchase_date;
options.explanation: This query is incorrect because BETWEEN selects books inside the 500-to-1000 range, the opposite of the required price condition. It also sorts purchase dates ascending instead of descending.

questions.answerExplanation: This query is correct. NOT BETWEEN 500 AND 1000 selects prices below 500 or above 1000. The date condition selects purchases before January 17, 2007, and DESC sorts the newest qualifying purchase first. This query is highlighted in the source document, but it is technically invalid. The expression OR 1000 does not provide a Boolean condition; it should be OR price > 1000.
questions.technicalNote: The correction document highlights A and C. Choice C is syntactically invalid because `OR 1000` is not a Boolean condition, while Choice B is the technically correct second query. Scoring follows the document-highlighted answers A and C as requested.

questions.stem: Which two queries will return the string Hello! We're ready?

sections.title: Required output
sections.content:
Hello! We're ready
The apostrophe in We're must be represented correctly inside the Oracle character literal.

options.text: SELECT 'Hello! We're ready' FROM dual;
options.explanation: The apostrophe in We're prematurely closes the character literal, causing a syntax error.

options.text: SELECT 'Hello! We''re ready' ESCAPE '\' FROM dual;
options.explanation: Doubling the apostrophe correctly escapes it, but the ESCAPE clause is not valid in this select-list expression.

options.text: SELECT q'[Hello! We're ready]' FROM dual;
options.explanation: Oracle’s alternative quoting syntax allows the apostrophe to appear inside the string without doubling it.

options.text: SELECT q'!Hello! We're ready!' FROM dual;
options.explanation: The exclamation mark is used as the alternative quote delimiter, so the embedded apostrophe is accepted.

options.text: SELECT 'Hello! We're ready' FROM dual;
options.explanation: The embedded apostrophe is not escaped, so the string literal is terminated incorrectly.

questions.answerExplanation: Oracle’s alternative quoting syntax allows the apostrophe to appear inside the string without doubling it. The exclamation mark is used as the alternative quote delimiter, so the embedded apostrophe is accepted.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the NVL, NVL2, and COALESCE functions?

options.text: NVL2 can have any number of expressions in its argument list.
options.explanation: NVL2 accepts exactly three expressions: the expression being tested, the value returned when non-null, and the value returned when null.

options.text: COALESCE stops evaluating its expression list when it finds the first non-null value.
options.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-null expression and uses short-circuit evaluation.

options.text: COALESCE stops evaluating its expression list when it finds the first null value.
options.explanation: COALESCE continues past null expressions and stops at the first non-null expression.

options.text: NVL can have any number of expressions in its argument list.
options.explanation: NVL accepts exactly two expressions.

options.text: NVL must have expressions of the same data-type group.
options.explanation: The two expressions must have compatible data types so Oracle can convert one to the other and return a consistent result type.

options.text: The first expression in NVL2 is never returned.
options.explanation: NVL2(expr1, expr2, expr3) tests expr1 but returns either expr2 or expr3. The source document nevertheless highlights only B and E as its expected answers.

questions.answerExplanation: COALESCE returns the first non-null expression and uses short-circuit evaluation. The two expressions must have compatible data types so Oracle can convert one to the other and return a consistent result type.
questions.technicalNote: The document highlights B and E. Choice F also accurately describes NVL2.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about Oracle interval data types?

options.text: INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND columns support fractions of seconds.
options.explanation: The seconds component of a day-to-second interval can include fractional seconds.

options.text: INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH columns support only monthly intervals within a single year.
options.explanation: A year-to-month interval can represent a duration containing multiple years and additional months.

options.text: INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH columns support monthly intervals within a range of years.
options.explanation: This interval type stores durations expressed using a combination of years and months.

options.text: The YEAR field in an INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH column must be a positive value.
options.explanation: Interval values may be positive or negative.

options.text: INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH columns support yearly intervals only.
options.explanation: The data type supports both year and month components, not only complete years.

options.text: A value in an INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND column can be copied into an INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH column.
options.explanation: The two interval types represent different units and are not directly interchangeable.

questions.answerExplanation: The seconds component of a day-to-second interval can include fractional seconds. This interval type stores durations expressed using a combination of years and months.
